source: Sweller, van Merrienboer & Paas (2019) Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later
finding: The 1998 model had three loads: intrinsic (element interactivity of the material given the learner's knowledge), extraneous (set by the instructional procedure) and germane (load needed to learn). The 1998 text treated germane load as substituting for extraneous load.
numbers: No new data. Restates the 1998 triad and the 2010 redefinition by Sweller.
quote: Germane cognitive load was defined as the cognitive load required to learn
limits: A review, not an experiment. Written by the theory's own proponents.
agent_relevance: The agent's prompt scaffold can change extraneous load (how the task is shown) but not the task's intrinsic load. Germane is the part nobody can set directly.

source: Sweller et al. (2019) Germane load redefined
finding: Current view: germane load is not an extra load. It redistributes working memory resources from extraneous activity to activity that deals with intrinsic load. Reason given: if germane simply replaced extraneous load, total load would not fall when extraneous load falls, yet many studies show it falls.
numbers: Departure from 1998 stated explicitly in the paper.
quote: germane cognitive load has a redistributive function from extraneous to intrinsic aspects of the task
limits: A definitional repair. Critics (Kalyuga 2011, de Jong 2010) say it makes germane untestable as its own construct.
agent_relevance: For an LLM, germane reduces to: remove distracting context so the tokens left go to the task. There is no separate germane knob.

source: Sweller et al. (2019) Variability effect and the origin of germane load
finding: The germane idea came from Paas and van Merrienboer (1994) variability result: high variability helped transfer when learners studied worked examples (low load) but hurt when they solved conventional problems (high load). Designs that cut extraneous load may work better if they add germane processing, provided total load stays within limits.
numbers: Interaction of problem format (worked vs conventional) by variability (low vs high). Cell means not read (original PDF blocked by Cloudflare).
limits: The review later files variability under intrinsic load. Original paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Varied examples help only when the agent has spare capacity. Adding variety to an already overloaded prompt may hurt.

source: Sweller et al. (2019) Goal-free effect, the oldest CLT effect
finding: Sweller and Levine (1982): conventional goal problems force means-ends analysis, which costs working memory and has little to do with schema building. Goal-free problems ('calculate as many variables as you can') cut load and focus on forward steps, which suits schema building.
numbers: Example used: car accelerated from rest for 1 min to 2 km/min. Original 1982 and 1988 counts not read.
limits: Later work (not read here) says the effect fades with expertise or very high element interactivity.
agent_relevance: Explicit goal pursuit (backward search) is costly. A scaffold stage that derives forward facts before aiming at the target resembles the goal-free format (link: forward and backward reasoning, in parallel run).

source: Sweller et al. (2019) Self-explanation prompts, imagination and capacity
finding: Worked examples with self-explanation prompts can beat worked examples without prompts, provided total load stays within capacity. Variability helps learners compare examples. Imagination instructions beat study instructions only once the learner knows enough to imagine.
numbers: Cites Renkl et al. 1998 (self-explanation, variability) and Cooper et al. 2001 (imagination). No numbers in this review.
limits: Conditional on capacity and expertise (expertise reversal).
agent_relevance: Prompting the agent to explain each step is the nearest germane manipulation. It costs tokens and may help only when the task is within the model's reach.

source: Sweller et al. (2019) Effort as an invalid learning cue
finding: De Bruin and van Merrienboer (2017): learners use high effort as a cue that they learned a lot. A more valid germane cue is being able to explain the solution to a peer. Teachers should prompt 'explain it', not 'was it hard'.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: A proposal, not a tested result in this paper.
agent_relevance: Do not treat long, effortful reasoning as evidence of learning. Use a checkable explanation or test as the cue (links: metacognition, testing effect).

source: Sweller et al. (2019) Subjective load scale limits
finding: Paas (1992) 9-point mental effort scale gives one overall load number (intrinsic plus extraneous) and cannot split the types. One rating after a whole phase was always higher than the average of ratings after each task (van Gog et al. 2012; Schmeck et al. 2015).
numbers: Scale: 9 points. Single end rating higher than mean of per-task ratings.
limits: Self-report. Researchers use different labels and scale lengths, which hurts comparability.
agent_relevance: No human self-report scale applies to a model. Any load proxy must come from behaviour (token count, error rate, attention).

source: Sweller (2023) The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories
finding: Germane load was not generated from data. It was added as a plausible idea. Over the years there were many extraneous and several intrinsic effects but no germane effects, so germane is now the working memory resources used for intrinsic rather than extraneous load and is no longer an independent source of load.
numbers: No effect size. A statement about the status of the construct.
quote: no instructional consequences of germane cognitive load have been identified
limits: Written by the founder. It admits the 1998 germane claim lacked an empirical base.
agent_relevance: Do not add an operator to the schema that tries to increase germane load. Section 4b (not to add) can cite this.

source: Sweller (2023) Replication failures drove the intrinsic/extraneous split
finding: The intrinsic/extraneous split was introduced when cognitive load effects seemed to appear and disappear. Failures to replicate (mostly conceptual replications) were traced to element interactivity and expertise reversal. Each failure led to theory change rather than rejection.
numbers: Cites the replication crisis (Open Science Collaboration 2015). No count of failed replications in the text read.
limits: Can be read as post-hoc rescue of the theory. Sweller frames it as theory development.
agent_relevance: Effect sizes of load manipulations depend on task complexity and expertise. Expect the same for prompt-level manipulations on a model: test per difficulty band.

source: Kalyuga (2011) Cognitive Load Theory: How Many Types of Load Does It Really Need?
finding: Argues traditional germane load is indistinguishable from intrinsic load. Germane was added from theory, not from results that needed it. The activities tied to it (self-explanation, imagination, variability) needed methods outside CLT. A two-type model is enough and makes the theory's boundaries clear.
numbers: Abstract and reference list only: article is paywalled.
quote: germane load is essentially indistinguishable from intrinsic load
limits: Only the abstract was opened. A redefined germane (resources spent on intrinsic load) is allowed as a possible role.
agent_relevance: Supports treating 'make the model reason more deeply' as raising intrinsic load toward a deeper goal, which must fit the budget.

source: Sweller (2010) Element interactivity and intrinsic, extraneous and germane cognitive load
finding: Element interactivity defines intrinsic load and also extraneous load. Germane load is defined in terms of intrinsic load, so it too relates to element interactivity.
numbers: Abstract only. Page shows 1798 citations.
limits: Paywalled, abstract only.
agent_relevance: Element interactivity is the one quantity that could be counted on a prompt or task (items that must be held together).

source: Leppink, Paas, van der Vleuten, van Gog & van Merrienboer (2013) Development of an instrument for measuring different types of cognitive load
finding: A 10-item scale (3 intrinsic, 3 extraneous, 4 germane) gave a three-component solution in a statistics lecture and CFA confirmed it in three more lectures. In the randomised experiment, only the germane-intended scale was entered as a predictor of posttest score along with prior knowledge, and prior knowledge was the strong predictor.
numbers: Study I n=56 PCA; II-III n=171, 136, 148 CFA; IV n=58 randomised (text-then-formula vs formula-then-text). Posttest mean 1.97 of 5, alpha .79. Prior knowledge linear effect F(1,24)=8.973, p<.01, eta2=.134. Logistic-regression lecture: IL-EL r=.61, IL-GL r=-.36, EL-GL r=-.56.
limits: Factor correlations differed between lectures (another lecture: IL-GL .04, EL-GL -.11). Germane items ask how much explanations helped learning, so they may measure perceived learning.
agent_relevance: An LLM judge rating 'did the explanation help' is the same kind of item and shares this validity problem.

source: Leppink et al. (2014) follow-up studies (secondary report in Leppink & van den Heuvel 2015 and Jiang & Kalyuga 2020)
finding: Two follow-up experiments separated intrinsic from extraneous load but failed to support the third factor as germane: 'support ... is limited'. The third factor was reinterpreted as intrinsic, extraneous and a subjective judgment of learning.
numbers: Numbers are in the 2014 paper, which was not opened. Secondary reports only.
quote: support for the assumption that the third factor in the psychometric instrument represents or closely relates to germane cognitive load is limited
limits: Secondary citation only.
agent_relevance: The germane factor in questionnaires tracks perceived learning, not a distinct resource.

source: Leppink & van den Heuvel (2015) The evolution of cognitive load theory and its application to medical education
finding: Argues for a two-factor framework because germane load has 'never really found support in empirical research'. Cites Lafleur et al.: a whole-task hypothesis-driven exam (somewhat higher intrinsic load) gave better diagnostic reasoning than a part-task OSCE. Very easy tasks give little germane activity (boredom).
numbers: Lafleur et al. randomised trial described without numbers.
limits: A review. It treats the intrinsic load to learning link as non-linear.
agent_relevance: Aim task difficulty just under overload. Easy tasks do not need a deep scaffold.

source: Jiang & Kalyuga (2020) Confirmatory factor analysis of cognitive load ratings supports a two-factor model
finding: Twelve Leppink-style items (4 intrinsic, 4 extraneous, 4 germane) fit a two-factor model when the germane items were treated as extra intrinsic indicators (reverse coded).
numbers: N=60 first-year EFL students, airport check-in dialogue in three phases. chi2=54.069, df=53, p=.433; CFI=.994; TLI=.993; RMSEA=.018; SRMR=.077; alpha=.78. One item loading .28.
limits: Small N. The germane items were assumed intrinsic, so it is not an independent test of the three-factor model. One domain; reuse of data from a modality study.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a scaffold needs only two dials: task complexity and presentation noise.

source: Klepsch, Schmitz & Seufert (2017) Development and validation of two instruments measuring intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load
finding: Counter-evidence: an 8-item naive rating (2 intrinsic, 3 extraneous, 3 germane) fit a three-factor model best in Study 2. Original germane items failed in Study 1 (low and high germane tasks rated 4.68 vs 4.88, p=.84). Revised items did separate tasks.
numbers: Study 1 N=97 (informed n=48, naive n=49), 24 tasks. Study 2 N=65 to 95 per task, 17 tasks. 3-factor CFA: chi2(221)=335.1, TLI=.951, CFI=.970, RMSEA=.021, AIC 845.1 vs 861.9 for 2-factor plus method factor; 1-factor TLI=.418. Alphas: ICL .81, ECL .86, GCL .67 (3 items) or .85 (2 items). Germane revised: t(76)=3.39, p<.01, d=0.35. Informed-rating alpha .25.
quote: we prefer GCL to be considered as a separable factor
limits: Read only the first 100k of 159k characters. Germane-performance correlation not seen. Germane items ask about effort and benefit, so may be perceived learning.
agent_relevance: The factor-analytic dispute is not settled: authors keep germane as a separable factor.

source: Debue & van de Leemput (2014) What does germane load mean? An empirical contribution to the cognitive load theory
finding: Online newspaper reading study. Germane rating did not predict retention. Performance was highest for text plus pictures and lower for text-pictures-animations and text only, yet load ratings did not differ between versions.
numbers: Phase 1 N=92: F(2,91)=5.605, eta2=.112; means TP .65 (SD .23), TPA .52 (SD .17), TO .50 (SD .18). Phase 2 N=36 eye tracking. Whole sample N=128: EL-GL r=-.470; IL-EL r=.277; GL-performance r=.045 (alternative GL2 r=.06), both ns; focused immersion-performance r=.237; GL positively related to cognitive absorption.
limits: Adapted Leppink items. The authors say ratings could not tell load types apart across versions and that GL may reflect motivation.
agent_relevance: The germane rating is not a predictor of outcome here and may pick up motivation. A model has no such motivation to calibrate.

source: Skulmowski & Xu (2022) Understanding cognitive load in digital and online learning
finding: Compares the 1998 additive model, the 2019 model (germane processing, not a load component) and a cost-benefit model in which some extraneous load buys germane processing (motivation, immersion). The same information can be extraneous for experts and intrinsic for novices.
numbers: No new numbers. Notes Jiang & Kalyuga 2020 and Fig. 1 comparing the three models.
limits: The cost-benefit view is a proposal. It implies extraneous load cannot be judged without knowing the intended test.
agent_relevance: Extra structure can pay off only if it feeds what is scored. Justify each added scaffold text by the target outcome.

source: Skulmowski & Xu (2022) on Mayer (2014) and generative processing
finding: Mayer (2014) argued that features that look like extra information or difficulty may raise generative (germane) processing through motivation, so such design may be fine if learners are not constantly overloaded as theory assumed.
numbers: No numbers in the passage read.
limits: Motivation, load and performance are said to interact in a more complex way than assumed.
agent_relevance: Do not assume all added prompt text is harmful. Measure on the benchmark.

source: Shang et al. (2025) United Minds or Isolated Agents? Coordination of LLMs under Cognitive Load Theory (CoThinker)
finding: Uses intrinsic and extraneous load as a design analogy, not a mechanism. Multi-agent coordination lifts math and reasoning but loses on instruction following. The paper does not frame the agent split as germane load.
numbers: LiveBench: Flash-8B Math 33.8 to 37.7, Language 16.1 to 29.4, Instruction 84.3 to 68.1; Pro Math 60.9 to 75.3. GPT-5 Reasoning 68.38 to 81.88. 16 of 25 paired comparisons pass Holm-Bonferroni at .05; the three significant losses are instruction following. Attention entropy 4.44, 4.80, 5.04 for task levels 1 to 3.
quote: a design analogy rather than a mechanistic claim
limits: Read via a page extract (first 100k of 201k characters). Authors call the link 'a design analogy rather than a mechanistic claim'.
agent_relevance: Load language motivates multi-agent splits, with gains on hard tasks and losses on easy ones. Keep the heavy scaffold off low-complexity tasks.

source: CogniLoad (2025) benchmark with tunable length, intrinsic difficulty and distractor density
finding: The only LLM benchmark here that names germane load. It uses task length N as a proxy for germane-like sustained schema maintenance, difficulty d for intrinsic load and needle-to-hay ratio for extraneous load. Length is the dominant failure driver.
numbers: 22 reasoning LLMs; 100 puzzles per (d,N,rho) config for 13 open models (14,000 per model), 10 per config for Gemini-2.5, gpt-5, R1-0528. 32K max context. d in {1,3,5,7,10}, N in {20,50,100,250}. At N=250 only gpt-5 (0.76) and o3 (0.68) pass 50%. DS-Llama-70B 0.89 to 0.66 and Qwen3-8B 0.71 to 0.40 from N=20 to 50. By d=5, 12 of 22 models under 50%. gpt-5 d=1 1.00, d=10 0.82. Distractor ratio gives a U-shape, worst at 25-50% relevant.
quote: task length (N ) serves as an operational proxy for conditions demanding germane load
limits: The germane mapping is the authors' choice and untested. Length confounds with context burden. gpt-5 at medium effort.
agent_relevance: Sustained state tracking over many steps is the main limit. Supports periodic state summary (re-chunking) in the scaffold.

source: CogniLoad (2025) regression and capacity thresholds
finding: A binomial logistic regression on d, log10 N and a quadratic in the relevant ratio gave negative significant d and N effects for every model. The U-shape in distractor ratio held for most models. gpt-5 and o3 have effective context length (ECL50) above 300 statements.
numbers: Quadratic term improved AIC for 18 of 22 models. Example: gemini-2.5-pro intercept 22.51, N coefficient -9.15; gpt-5 d coefficient -0.39, N -5.11; Qwen3-1.7B never reaches 50%.
limits: Synthetic puzzles only.
agent_relevance: A cheap way to find our agent's own capacity point: fit the same curve on our items and keep scaffold steps below the 50% length.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Beyond Accuracy: A Cognitive Load Framework for Tool-use Agents (ToolLoad-Bench)
finding: Models only intrinsic load (Tool Interaction Graph complexity) and extraneous load (ambiguity, distractor tools). No germane term. Accuracy decays as exp(-(k*CL_total + b)), and the fit passes a Hosmer-Lemeshow calibration test.
numbers: GPT-4o 68.0% overall; xLAM2-32B 78.8% best; Llama3.3-70B 23% even at low load. At high load only xLAM2-32B stays above 60%. Intrinsic weight set to 1; extraneous scaled by the ratio of accuracy drops.
limits: Benchmark built by the authors, so load scores are partly circular. k and b values not extracted.
agent_relevance: A two-dial model (intrinsic, extraneous) predicts agent success, in line with the dyadic view.

source: Chen et al. (2023) element interactivity as a measure of task complexity
finding: Element interactivity is the concepts or procedures that must be processed together. It depends on the learner's expertise: 'dog' is three elements to a novice reader and one to an expert. It underlies both intrinsic and extraneous load.
numbers: Only the introduction was read.
limits: Counting method not extracted.
agent_relevance: For a model, expertise is fixed by weights, but the number of interacting elements per step can be bounded.

source: Sweller et al. (2019) / Skulmowski & Xu (2022) summary of the model change
finding: 1998: total load = intrinsic + extraneous + germane, additive, with germane able to fill free capacity. 2019: germane is the share of working memory resources devoted to intrinsic load, so only intrinsic and extraneous are basic categories.
numbers: Skulmowski & Xu Fig. 1 compares 1998, 2019 and cost-benefit models.
limits: A verbal model. No fitted quantitative model of germane load was found.
agent_relevance: There is no computational germane model to port. Only the CogniLoad and ToolLoad curves are formal.
